strengths: Provides formal finite-sample guarantees (Theorem 2.1) for LLM-based pairwise evaluation under exchangeability, addressing a critical gap where naive baselines violate risk constraints (Table 3)

BPE is a simple yet effective uncertainty estimator that achieves superior calibration (ECE) and discrimination (AUROC/AUPRC) compared to predictive probability, verbalized confidence, and simulated annotators with only 2 forward passes

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena) and 4 model scales with 1000 random splits, demonstrating consistent risk control (empirical risk ≈ 0.097-0.099 at α=0.10)
Addresses a timely and important problem: as LLMs increasingly serve as evaluators in benchmarks and RL, reliability guarantees are essential for trustworthy model development
Clear presentation with well-motivated methodology, thorough appendices supporting reproducibility (prompts, hyperparameters, infrastructure details), and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Critical dependence on exchangeability assumption between calibration and deployment data with no robustness analysis; no experiments with distribution shifts that would occur in practice across benchmarks or prompt variations

Very low coverage at strict risk budgets limits practical utility: Qwen-7B achieves only 0.018 coverage at α=0.05 on MT-Bench (Figure 2a); no practitioner guidance on selecting α or minimum acceptable coverage levels

BPE analysis is shallow: lacks ablations on why bidirectional aggregation helps versus simple entropy, no failure case analysis, and sometimes shows accuracy degradation (Table 1: MT-Bench Qwen-7B 0.731→0.738) without thorough investigation

Finite-sample correction tightness unexplored: the -1 in Eq. 5 is theoretically justified but empirical risk stays well below α (0.097-0.099 vs 0.10), suggesting potential conservatism; no sensitivity analysis on calibration set size effects
BPE is white-box only (requires logits/probabilities), limiting applicability to API-only models (GPT-4) that dominate practical LLM evaluation; no proposed solutions for black-box settings
Framework limited to binary pairwise judgments; extensions to ranking, rubric-based scoring, or open-ended evaluation deferred to future work, reducing generality for practical evaluation pipelines
Aggregation strategy (simple averaging in Eq. 2) not justified; no exploration of weighted averaging or detection of which ordering direction is more reliable for individual judgments
Incremental theoretical contribution building heavily on Wang et al. (2025a) linearization framework; main novelty is application to pairwise setting rather than fundamental methodological innovation
Figure 3 shows non-negligible variance across splits (±1σ bands), raising questions about individual deployment reliability even though mean risk tracks the target

Missing comparison details: simulated annotators sometimes match or exceed BPE on individual metrics (RewardBench Qwen-14B ROC: 0.880→0.809); computational cost-benefit trade-off not thoroughly analyzed

strengths: Sound theoretical contribution with valid finite-sample FDR guarantees via proper application of conformal prediction theory to pairwise judgment
Exceptional experimental rigor: 1000 random splits, 5 benchmarks, 4 model scales, comprehensive ablations including label noise robustness and cross-benchmark transfer
Practical deployment value: drop-in calibration layer requiring only logits, no retraining, works on both general and specialized judges (Skywork-Critic)
Thorough empirical validation showing consistent satisfaction of risk bounds (empirical FDR ≈ 0.097–0.099 at α=0.10) with proper statistical methodology
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, intuitive Figure 1, and extensive reproducibility details enabling proper implementation
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: core risk control mechanism (linearized loss, Eqs. 4-6) directly adapted from Wang et al. (2025b); Theorem 2.1 follows standard conformal arguments with minimal novel technical content

BPE design choices lack theoretical or empirical justification: no ablations comparing simple averaging to alternatives (max, min, weighted schemes); binary entropy application ad-hoc with no analysis of why it correlates with position-robust decisions
Severe practical coverage limitations: MT-Bench achieves only 24.6% coverage at α=0.10 for Qwen-7B (Table 3); JudgeBench drops to 2.3% at α=0.05 (Table 5); no analysis of which judgment types abstain

Fragile exchangeability assumption undermines practical deployment: Table 12 shows cross-benchmark calibration transfer fails dramatically (risk up to 0.20 on RewardBench→MT-Bench), yet no guidance on detecting or mitigating distribution shift

Modest improvements over Trust-or-Escalate (Jung et al., 2025): SCOPE achieves only 1.1–3.2× higher coverage (Table 7), with gains primarily from continuous BPE signals rather than the risk control mechanism itself
BPE methodology underjustified: no analysis of how entropy correlates with position bias, how to distinguish genuine ambiguity from position disagreement, or ablation studies on aggregation choices
Label noise degradation: Table 10 shows coverage collapses to near-zero at 20% calibration set noise; unclear what noise levels are acceptable in practice with real human preferences
Limited scope: restricted to binary pairwise judgment, requires expensive ground-truth calibration data, prompt engineering effects unexplored, no downstream task validation
